reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Neuropathic pain arises from a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system and is distinct from nociceptive pain caused by ongoing tissue damage
Typical descriptors are burning, shooting, electric-shock, or stabbing pain, often with numbness, and it characteristically maps to a recognisable neuroanatomical distribution
Hallmark abnormal sensory findings include allodynia, where a normally non-painful stimulus causes pain, and hyperalgesia, an exaggerated response to a painful stimulus
Common causes span diabetic and other polyneuropathies, postherpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, radiculopathy, post-stroke central pain, spinal cord injury, and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy
Screening tools such as the DN4 or painDETECT can support recognition, but diagnosis rests on history, distribution, and confirmatory sensory examination

First-line pharmacological principles favour gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, with topical agents for localised pain and opioids generally avoided as first choice
A multimodal, multidisciplinary approach combining medication, physical therapy, psychological strategies, and treatment of the underlying cause gives the best results
Interventional options such as nerve blocks and neuromodulation may help selected patients with refractory pain
Realistic goals centre on partial pain reduction and improved function and sleep rather than complete pain relief
reference.pathophysiology: Neuropathic pain results from maladaptive changes throughout the nervous system after nerve injury or disease. Damaged neurons develop ectopic and spontaneous discharge and altered ion-channel expression, producing peripheral sensitisation. In the dorsal horn, increased excitability, loss of inhibitory interneuron function, and glial activation drive central sensitisation and wind-up. Structural and functional reorganisation extends to the brain, and descending modulatory pathways may shift toward facilitation of pain. These changes together explain the spontaneous pain, allodynia, and hyperalgesia that persist beyond any ongoing tissue injury.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed sensory examination mapping the distribution and testing for allodynia and hyperalgesia
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography where a peripheral nerve or root lesion is suspected
Screening questionnaires such as DN4 or painDETECT to support recognition
Targeted investigation of the underlying cause, for example glycaemic testing, imaging of the spine, or metabolic screening
Quantitative sensory testing or skin biopsy for small-fibre assessment in selected cases
redFlags: Progressive motor weakness, sphincter disturbance, or saddle anaesthesia suggesting cord or cauda equina compression
Rapidly worsening deficit implying an evolving compressive or inflammatory lesion
Systemic features such as weight loss or night pain raising concern for malignancy or infection
New severe pain with fever suggesting an infective or inflammatory neurological process
reference.prognosis: Neuropathic pain is often chronic and only partially responsive to treatment, but many patients achieve meaningful reductions in pain intensity and improved function with a structured multimodal approach. Prognosis is better when a reversible underlying cause is identified and treated early.
pitfalls: Treating neuropathic pain with conventional analgesics or NSAIDs alone, which are usually ineffective
Escalating opioids for a pain type that responds poorly to them and carries dependence risk
Missing a serious underlying cause such as cord compression or malignancy
Setting an expectation of complete pain relief rather than functional improvement
Neglecting the psychological and sleep dimensions that amplify chronic neuropathic pain
management: Identify and treat any reversible underlying cause, such as optimising glycaemic control in diabetic neuropathy or decompressing a compressed nerve root
Start first-line pharmacotherapy with a gabapentinoid, a tricyclic antidepressant or a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor such as duloxetine, titrating to effect
Use topical agents such as lidocaine or capsaicin for localised peripheral neuropathic pain
Reserve opioids such as tramadol as later-line options given limited long-term benefit and harms, avoiding them as first choice
Consider syndrome-specific agents, such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine for trigeminal neuralgia
Combine pharmacotherapy with physiotherapy, psychological therapy and a multimodal self-management approach
Refer to a specialist pain service for interventional options such as nerve blocks or neuromodulation when pain is refractory
Set realistic functional goals and review efficacy and adverse effects regularly, rotating or combining agents as needed

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Neuropathic pain

nodes.text: Burning, shooting or electric-shock pain with numbness after a nerve lesion or disease
Red flag present (progressive weakness, sphincter loss, saddle anaesthesia)?
Urgent spinal imaging and surgical review for cord or cauda equina compression
Sensory mapping, allodynia testing, nerve studies, DN4 or painDETECT, imaging
Neuropathic features with a lesion in the somatosensory system?
Consider nociceptive, complex regional or centralised pain; reassess
Treat any reversible cause such as diabetic glycaemia or nerve compression
Avoid relying on NSAIDs or escalating opioids
Often chronic and partly responsive; a structured multimodal approach improves function
